title: Optimal operating temperature for industry-compatible silicon spin quantum computing: colder is not necessarily better
authors: Paul Steinacker, Amanda E. Seedhouse, Nard Dumoulin Stuyck, Tuomo Tanttu, MengKe Feng, Santiago Serrano, Ensar Vahapoglu, Samuel K. Bartee, Philip Y. Mai, Alexis Shaw, Andreas Nickl, Sebastian Pauka, Brendan Harlech-Jones, Juan P. Dehollain, Fay E. Hudson, Kok Wai Chan, Thomas A. Ohki, David Reilly, Christopher C. Escott, Chih Hwan Yang, Wee Han Lim, Arne Laucht, Andre Saraiva, Andrew S. Dzurak, Jared H. Cole
abstract: Silicon spin qubits are a leading candidate for large-scale quantum computing owing to their compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. However, scaling to useful fault-tolerant processors will likely generate thermal loads that exceed the cooling power available at millikelvin temperatures. Raising the operating temperature eases cooling requirements but reduces gate fidelity, increasing the overhead of quantum error correction. Identifying the operating temperature that minimizes total power consumption is therefore a key challenge for commercially viable quantum computers. Here, we use gate set tomography to benchmark two-qubit silicon chips fabricated in both industrial and academic environments over a range of temperatures. Elevated temperatures substantially shorten coherence times and increase gate and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelities. Based on these measurements, we develop a general power model for silicon quantum computers that combines cryogenic cooling requirements with error-correction overheads. We show that a finite optimal operating temperature exists and is strongly influenced by a crossover temperature near 1 K in current devices, above which gate fidelity degrades rapidly. These results connect device-level fidelity limitations to system-level power requirements, providing design guidelines for large-scale silicon quantum computers.
summary: This work investigates the operational sweet spot for silicon spin qubits, challenging the assumption that colder temperatures are always best. By modeling the total power budget—which includes cryogenic cooling needs and error correction overheads—the authors show a finite optimal temperature exists near 1 K. This provides critical design guidelines for building large-scale, commercially viable quantum computers.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the optimal operating temperature for silicon spin qubits that minimizes total power consumption by balancing cryogenic cooling costs against the overheads required by quantum error correction.
main_result: A finite, non-zero optimal operating temperature exists, strongly influenced by a crossover temperature near 1 K; above this point, gate fidelity degrades rapidly due to environmental noise sources.
method: The authors used Gate Set Tomography (GST) to benchmark two-qubit chips across various temperatures and developed a general power model combining cooling requirements with QEC overheads.
model_or_system: The physical system is silicon spin qubits, which are highly compatible with semiconductor manufacturing. The analysis models the temperature dependence of gate infidelity using power-law fits ($M \propto [1 + (T/T_X)^n]^{-1}$).
key_observables: Gate and SPAM fidelities, coherence times ($T_1$, $T_{	ext{Ramsey}}^2$), total operational power consumption.
important_parameters: Optimal operating temperature, crossover temperature ($T_X \approx 0.5-1$ K), low-temperature infidelity ($\kappa$), and the error correction overhead scaling factor.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that minimizing total power requires jointly considering computational performance (fidelity) and energy use (cooling/QEC).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate fidelity vs. temperature, coherence times vs. temperature, and critically, the trade-off between cryogenic cooling power and error correction power as a function of operating temperature.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the conflict between low temperatures (high fidelity) and high operational costs (cooling/QEC). It then presents experimental measurements using GST across multiple devices to fit temperature dependencies. Finally, it develops and analyzes a comprehensive power model to pinpoint the optimal finite operating temperature.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, device-level guidelines for scaling quantum processors by quantifying the energy trade-off inherent in achieving fault tolerance, which is crucial for any physical implementation of quantum computation.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
